subject: Liu et al. (2003)
object: Liu et al. (2003) used immunogold electron microscopy in rodents to localize Neph1 to the glomerular slit diaphragm. They showed that Neph1 interacted directly with 2 other slit diaphragm components, nephrin and ZO-1. Both native and recombinant Neph1 associated with each other as dimers and multimers. Neph1 bound nephrin through the extracellular segments, and this interaction was specific: neither protein interacted with P-cadherin. ZO-1 bound the cytoplasmic tail of Neph1 through its PDZ domains.

subject: Liu et al. (2003)
object: Liu et al. (2003) disrupted the Neph1-nephrin interaction in vivo by injecting rodents with combinations of anti-Neph1 and anti-nephrin antibodies, each given at a dose too low to cause nephritis on its own. The animals developed proteinuria that did not depend on complement or leukocytes, and their podocyte foot processes were preserved. Podocyte Neph1 and nephrin protein levels fell modestly and ZO-1 protein fell dramatically, with no change in the mRNA levels of any of the 3 genes. The authors concluded that the nephrin-Neph1 interaction appears to be an important determinant of glomerular permeability.

subject: Solanki et al. (2019)
object: Solanki et al. (2019) reported that homozygous mutations in KIRREL1, a slit diaphragm component, cause steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS), and concluded that KIRREL1 has an important role in modulating the integrity of the slit diaphragm and maintaining glomerular filtration function.

subject: Solanki et al. (2019)
object: Solanki et al. (2019) described a boy (A666_21) from a consanguineous family who was diagnosed with nephrotic syndrome at age 5 years, was steroid-resistant at initial presentation, and was resistant to various immunosuppressive drugs, never achieving complete remission and having undulating proteinuria with only partial response; ACE inhibitor and ARB treatment was not beneficial, but renal function remained normal over 12.5 years of follow-up. Renal biopsy showed minor mesangial hypercellularity consistent with minimal change disease. A younger sister had periorbital edema and proteinuria, and extended relatives included 3 children with ESRD and 1 with nephrotic syndrome, but their genotypes were unknown. There were no extrarenal manifestations.

subject: Solanki et al. (2019)
object: Solanki et al. (2019) described a boy of Italian descent (B742_21) from a consanguineous family who was diagnosed with nephrotic syndrome at age 14 years and was steroid-resistant at presentation. He had hypertension and achieved complete remission on tacrolimus, a calcium channel blocker, and ACE inhibitor, but over 4 years of follow-up developed progressive chronic kidney disease (CKD stage 2). Renal biopsy showed focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, and electron microscopy showed extensive podocyte foot process effacement, increased mesangial matrix and mesangial proliferation. There were no extrarenal or syndromic features.

subject: Solanki et al. (2019)
object: By whole-exome sequencing and homozygosity mapping in 596 individuals from 406 families with SRNS, Solanki et al. (2019) identified homozygous KIRREL1 missense mutations in 2 individuals from unrelated consanguineous families (frequency 2/406, 0.4%). Both residues were conserved to zebrafish and lay within homozygosity peaks on chromosome 1.

subject: Solanki et al. (2019)
object: In patient A666_21 with SRNS, Solanki et al. (2019) identified a homozygous p.Arg440Cys missense mutation in KIRREL1, located within the maximum NPL homozygosity peak on chromosome 1; the allele had a gnomAD minor allele frequency of 3.97 x 10(-6).

subject: Solanki et al. (2019)
object: In patient B742_21, of Italian descent, Solanki et al. (2019) identified a homozygous p.Ser573Leu missense mutation in KIRREL1 within the maximum homozygosity peak on chromosome 1. This variant had a gnomAD MAF of 7.87 x 10(-4), an allele frequency of 0.0011 in Europeans, and was found in the homozygous state in one gnomAD control; the authors suggested possible incomplete penetrance or variable expressivity but considered in silico, conservation and functional data conclusive of its impact.

subject: Solanki et al. (2019)
object: Solanki et al. (2019) found that Flag-tagged KIRREL1 Arg440Cys and Ser573Leu mutants stably expressed in human podocytes mislocalized, with reduced membrane fraction levels and increased localization in Golgi, early endosomes and lysosomes compared with wildtype, suggesting trafficking defects; NPHS1 membrane localization was unaffected. Podocyte monolayers expressing the mutants showed significantly increased albumin flux, indicating impaired intercellular integrity.
